max_tire.note: Fits a stock 88 or 109 once the steering stops are adjusted so the tyre clears the chassis at full lock. 215/85R16 is also close to the 7.50x16 size; 265/75R16 on 5.5 in rims rubbed the frame for one owner. Original rims are tube-type; fit tubeless tyres only on rims with safety humps.

timeline.change: Launched at the Amsterdam Motor Show: 80-inch wheelbase, 1.6 petrol
Freewheel 4WD replaced by selectable four-wheel drive via a dog clutch (1950–51)
Larger 2.0 petrol replaces the 1.6 (1950–52, sources differ)
Wheelbases grow to 86/107, then 88/109 in 1956; 2.0 diesel follows in 1957
Series II: wider 'barrel side' body and 2.25 petrol
Series IIA: 2.25 diesel; 2.6 six in the 109 from 1967
Headlamps move into the wings on home-market IIAs (February)
Series III: all-synchro gearbox, plastic grille and new dash
Factory sales to North America end
Stage 1 V8 (3.5 Rover V8, permanent 4WD), mostly 109s
Axles and hubs strengthened (1980); half-shaft splines go from 10 to 24 (1982)
Series production ends; the coil-sprung One Ten (1983) and Ninety (1984) replace it

identify.intro: Series trucks were built for 37 years, in several countries, and plenty have been rebuilt from mixed parts. The chassis number tells you what you're actually buying.

items.head: Chassis number (pre-1979)
items.body: Stamped on an aluminium plate, on the bulkhead inside the cab on earlier trucks and under the bonnet on later ones. The first three digits give model, body and engine: 241–245 is a IIA 88 petrol, 251–255 a IIA 109 petrol, 901–905 a Series III 88 petrol, 911–915 a Series III 109 petrol.

items.head: 17-character VIN (late 1979 on)
items.body: Land Rover switched to 17-character VINs at the end of 1979. Glencoyne's examples: LBCAH… is a Series III 109 petrol, LBAAG… a Series III 88 diesel.

items.head: Which Series is it?
items.body: Series I (1948–58) has flat sides. Series II (1958–61) has the wider barrel-side body. IIA (1961–71) looks almost the same, and late home-market IIAs have headlamps in the wings. Series III (1971–85) has a plastic grille and a plastic dash with instruments in front of the driver.

items.head: NADA trucks and licence-builds
items.body: Only 811 long-wheelbase 2.6 six IIAs were NADA (North American Dollar Area) trucks. Bring a Trailer also sells many Spanish-built Santana and Colombian 'Ensambladora Automotriz' 88s and 109s, so confirm the maker.

items.head: Heritage certificate
items.body: The British Motor Museum's Heritage Certificates cover Land Rovers from 1948 on and copy the factory ledger: build and despatch dates, engine number, colour and equipment.

capability.note: AULRO owners; best about 21 mpg at a steady 50 mph in a SWB
60–65 mph on the flat with a Fairey overdrive, per Rovers North forum members

values.intro: Series values have kept climbing, according to Hagerty, and in its 2019 analysis petrol trucks and soft-tops commanded slightly more than diesels and wagons.
values.note: Based on Bring a Trailer sold results in 2025–26: 18 Series 88s ($11,000–56,000, median about $26,500) and 11 Series 109s ($15,000–56,000, median $25,500). Hagerty found petrol trucks worth about 6% more than diesels and soft-tops about 2% more than wagons.

paragraphs: Factory sales to North America ended in 1974, so most Series trucks in the US today are private imports. Every Series truck is now well past NHTSA's 25-year line, so FMVSS isn't a barrier. On EPA Form 3520-1, code E exempts vehicles at least 21 years old in original configuration; a truck with a non-original engine can't use that exemption unless the replacement is the same engine model.

California is the catch. Gasoline vehicles of the 1975 model year and older are smog-exempt, but a non-California-certified direct import from 1975 on is supposed to pass a CARB laboratory test for a Certificate of Conformance. Rovers North forum members trying to register a 1978 Series III were told by ARB that the truck would need modifying and testing to 1978 California standards. Pre-1976 petrol trucks are the easy route there.

production.intro: The Series ran from 1948 to 1985 and was overwhelmingly an export product.
